sections.name: Edit a road
help: Pick a road, or click any part of one in the model.

Branch off this one closes the panel; click on the road it leaves from — the cursor snaps to the centreline, so a junction forms there — then click where it goes, as many points as you like, and it runs through them as a curve. Enter or double-click finishes; Esc takes back the last point. From my lines instead takes something you have already drawn with any SketchUp tool — Line, Arc, Freehand, a bezier — so a road can be any shape at all. Select what you drew, then press the button. Road from a face I drew goes further still: draw the asphalt itself as a face, whatever shape it has to be, select it and press the button, and the kerb, verge, footway, parking and edge line of the style set below are laid round its edge. The shape is yours, so there is no junction to solve and no corner to argue with. A hole in the face is treated as an island and is kerbed on its inside. It becomes its own group that no rebuild touches; right-click it to pick any style from the library without touching the panel, so one drawing can hold a dozen face roads of a dozen kinds. It is built flat, as a road is; the same box will smooth it if you want the facets of a rolling face blended instead. Draw the next road as a face against the first — any width, any style — and where the two share an edge the curb, verge, sidewalk and edge line all stop short of it on both sides, so the asphalt of one runs straight into the asphalt of the other with nothing in the way. The same box will curb it all the way round instead if you would rather. Markings, median and shoulder come with it: the lanes divide the width the face actually has at each point, so a face that narrows gets lanes that narrow with it. Set Lanes, Median and Shoulder below as for any road. The line the markings follow is worked out from the shape of the face; if it guesses wrong on an odd shape, draw a line down the road, select it with the road and right-click → Set the line its markings follow. Arrow in a lane and Crossing across a face road close the panel and ask for a click; the arrow box takes a direction, a count and a spacing, so each lane can point a different way. All of this is also on Extensions → TerraRoad → Convert face into road, which needs nothing selected: with one face road in the model it uses that one, and with several it asks you to click the one you mean.

Move a point bends the road, leaving both its ends exactly where they are; take hold of the centreline anywhere along its length. Type a height and press Enter to take that point up or down. Its name, its settings and its junctions with everything else are kept. Mirrored copy makes a reflected twin as a road of its own: draw the line of symmetry, select it, then press the button. To flip one road's own section left-for-right instead, right-click it in the model.

Everything under Roads is generated, and every rebuild remakes it — adding one road changes the kerb returns of its neighbours. Anything you model by hand goes in Manual Additions beside it, which no rebuild touches.

sections.name: Convert face into road

buttons.label: Convert to a road
buttons.title: Builds the selected face as a stretch of road: curb, verge and sidewalk round it, and the median, parking, lamp posts and markings the style asks for.

buttons.label: Convert to a junction
buttons.title: Builds the selected face as a junction: asphalt and nothing else. No median, no parking, no lamp posts, nothing painted, and open all the way round so the roads that meet it run straight in.

buttons.label: Cut it into separate components - roads, turns and junctions
Change the style of the selected road
buttons.title: Puts a different style on the face road you have selected, and rebuilds it to that style. Pick the road in the model or the Outliner first.

buttons.label: Repair the selected road or junction
buttons.title: Checks the road or junction you have SELECTED against its style - the asphalt, the width, the curb and footway, the median, and anything that has escaped outside the face - and builds it again if it is wrong. Says what it found. It touches nothing you have not picked.

buttons.label: Make this model lighter...
buttons.title: Most of a big road model is painted curb: a separate block of geometry every three feet, down both sides of every road and both sides of every median. On a large plan that is four fifths of everything in the model, and it is what makes SketchUp slow and what a live renderer like D5 chokes on. This asks once what you can do without - longer curb blocks or none, fewer studs or none, bay lines, lamp posts - and applies it to every road at once. It changes what is DRAWN, never a shape, a style or a width, and you can put any of it back the same way.

buttons.label: Build every road again to this version
buttons.title: Builds EVERY road and junction in the model again, to the version of TerraRoad that is loaded now. A road keeps the geometry it was built with, so anything fixed in a new version does not appear on work already in the model until that road is built again - this is what does it, in one press instead of one road at a time. Each goes back on what it is recorded as being: a road on the style it names, a junction on the roads that run into it. It asks first, because on a large plan it takes a while.

buttons.label: Road ↔ junction
buttons.title: Turns the piece you have SELECTED into the other thing: a road becomes a junction, a junction becomes a road. The shape and the style are untouched - a junction simply carries no lane markings, no parking and no median, because it has no middle to lay them along. Press it again to put it back.

buttons.label: Connect the junctions to the roads
buttons.title: Finds which pieces actually run into which, calls a piece with three or more of them a junction, and builds every one again with the joins it found: the curb, verge, footway and edge line stopping across each join and the asphalt carried out to meet, and the corners between the joins kept curbed and walked. Select a junction to do that one and the roads round it; select nothing to do the lot.

buttons.label: Break the selected group into components
Work it out from the face

help: Draw the asphalt as a face, select it, and convert. The curb, verge, sidewalk and edge line of the style below are laid round its edge; the shoulder, bay and median come out of the width you drew, and the lanes divide what is left. Update rebuilds them along with everything else.

Converting uses the style picked in STYLE at the top of this panel - press Apply there and the cross-section above shows exactly what will be built. The width of the road is taken from the face you drew, not from the style. The style says everything else - the curb, verge, footway, median and bay keep the sizes it gives them - and the asphalt takes up whatever difference there is.

Drawn your whole layout as one face? Cut it first. One face with every road in it has no line down the middle, so it gets no markings; nothing to meet, so no curb opens; and one style over roads of every width. Cutting gives each road, turn and junction its own named group in the Outliner — pick one and change it on its own, and where two meet the asphalt runs through.

One road per face: a junction has no line down the middle, so it is left unmarked and gets no bay. Draw each arm as its own face and let them meet — where two share an edge the curb opens and the asphalt runs straight through. The width you drew is measured and checked against the style; if they disagree you are told. Crown and superelevation do not apply — draw the face at the levels you want. All of this is on Extensions → TerraRoad too, and works with nothing selected.

buttons.label: Edit the roads in the model

help: A right-angle corner gets the first figure. Every degree gentler than a right angle adds the second, and every degree sharper takes it off — so a slight deflection is swept wide and a hard turn is cut tight, from one setting. At the default, a 90° corner is 25 ft, a 45° turn 70 ft, a 10° one 105 ft. The kerb, verge and footway follow, since they are offsets of the centreline. Set the second figure to 0 to give every corner the same radius. The tightest inside kerb below still wins wherever it is bigger.

Where a road of one type meets a road of another end to end, there is no junction — two lines meet and nothing branches — so each used to stop dead and leave one kerb facing the other across the difference in their widths. That stretch is now given over to a transition: every band of the one road is carried to its opposite number in the other, kerb to kerb, footway to footway. What the wider road has and the narrower has not — a median, a service road — fades in over the same length. Set it to 0 to leave the two roads to stop where they stop.

Adding one road to a design of thirty used to rebuild all thirty — a wait, and every group in the outliner thrown away and made again. With this on, a road is left exactly as it is unless something that shapes it has changed: where it goes, its section, the markers standing on it, or the junctions it is part of. So a new road rebuilds itself and the roads it joins, and nothing else. Turn it off to build the whole design every time.

Each road is cut where it starts and stops turning, and every piece becomes its own group inside it — Road 1 Straight 1, Road 1 Bend 2 and so on. A design that joins a 40 ft road to a 100 ft one can then pick the bend between them on its own. Pieces shorter than the figure are folded into the one before, since a road cut into slivers is worse than one group.

Right-click any piece of road in the model for a TerraRoad menu on it. Apply a style to this piece only changes that straight or that bend and nothing else — which is how a 40 ft road is joined to a 100 ft one. Below it are the same things for the whole road: apply a style to all of it, load its settings into the panel, or rename it. Put this piece back on the road settings undoes a piece style.

Press Edit the roads in the model and every corner of every road gets a grip. Drag one and the road follows — everything meeting that point comes with it, so junctions stay joined. Type a radius while the cursor is on a corner and that turn alone is cut to it, whatever the design-wide radius says; type 0 to put it back. Click a road anywhere else and the panel fills with that road's own settings. Red grips are corners and ends; blue ones are junctions — drag one of those and every road meeting it comes too, so the junction stays a junction. Shift takes the grip behind, for two carriageways sitting on top of each other. Esc finishes.

With Rebuild as soon as I move a centreline on, you can move the centrelines with SketchUp's own Move, Rotate or Scale and the roads rebuild themselves the moment you stop — no button to press. It waits for the movement to settle, so a drag that touches fifty lines rebuilds once.

Ticked, a right-angle corner comes round on the inside kerb — the one a vehicle actually tracks — at the road's own full width: a 40 ft road at 40 ft, a 100 ft one at 100 ft. The outside then falls where the road's width puts it, 80 ft and 200 ft. Change the lanes, the verge or the footway and the corner follows. Turns gentler than a right angle are swept wider still by the per-degree figure above.

It is set on the inside for a reason. Set on the outside, a 40 ft outer radius on a 40 ft road leaves the centreline at 20 ft and the inside at nothing — the two kerbs are the same number pulled in opposite directions, and only the inside one is what anybody means by a corner radius.
Untick it to set that inside radius yourself in the box, whatever the road width. 0 leaves every bend exactly as drawn.

There is one limit under this that is not a setting: a road cannot turn inside its own width, or the inner edge folds through itself and the faces invert. Half a foot is kept clear of that whatever is asked for, and the build says so when it has had to.

The second interval is used when the road is not draping onto terrain and not being graded — the drawn vertices already carry the curvature, so a big layout costs a fraction of the geometry. Corner radius rounds sharp corners only; drawn arcs are left alone. Bumps shorter than the max length are levelled by a straightedge dragged along the road, so real hills survive and mesh wrinkles do not.

rows.label: Let the road open out into the corner

fields.label: Let the road open out into the corner

fields.label: Carry a road that stops short onto the one it meets
Where two roads cross
options: Junction — pave it with kerb returns
Bridge — carry one road over the other
Plain crossing — paved through, square corners

rows.label: Ignore design speed — size curves from the road width alone

fields.label: Ignore design speed — size curves from the road width alone

rows.label: Curve the connection where roads of different width meet

fields.label: Curve the connection where roads of different width meet

rows.label: Truck apron width / how proud it sits
Turning head at every dead end

fields.label: Turning head at every dead end

help: Where two roads cross, this decides what is built there — a paved junction with kerb returns, or a roundabout with its island, truck apron, circulatory carriageway, splitter islands and yield lines. It happens wherever your centrelines meet; there is nothing to place by hand.

The asphalt widens along the corner curve as it comes in, rather than being held to one width and cut off square. Unfinished, and off for now: the corner the road takes over is not built with it, so where two roads cross their widened edges meet at a point with no curve and no chamfer between them. Leave it off unless you want to see what it does.

At 0, which is how it comes, every road meeting another is a junction: both are cut back and the corner between them carries the kerb, the verge and the footway round on a curve. Type an angle — 20 or so — and a road leaving at less than that is treated as branching instead: the road it leaves runs straight on unbroken, the kerb between the two stops where they overlap, and the ground between is paved as a gore. That is what a slip road wants and what an ordinary street junction does not.
A roundabout is not one of these: it is chosen above, under Where two roads cross, just above. These settings shape a paved junction.

Square corners are no longer offered. Two roads meeting square is not a thing that gets built: a kerb turns, and the footway turns with it. Where the radius asked for will not go, the corner is cut to the smallest curve that will.

On Crossings only, a T-junction is paved and its corners are rounded, but it gets no yellow box and no stop lines — which is why a T can look plainer than a crossroads. Choose Every join to mark them the same.

The narrower road is brought out to the wider one over the last of its length before the junction, so both arrive at the same section and the kerbs have something to meet. Without it the narrow road arrives at its own width and the kerb line steps sideways at the node.

The truck apron is the mountable ring just outside the central island, laid a little proud of the circulatory roadway so a car keeps off it and a lorry's back wheels can ride over it. The splitter island between the traffic going in and the traffic coming out is the road's own central median, carried on to the edge of the circulatory roadway — same width, same kerb, painted the same — so the two read as one island rather than the median stopping short behind a separate one. Give the road a median and it appears.

A proper connection, without the junction treatment. The legs are trimmed back and the space between them paved, so the two roads become one surface rather than two overlapping ones — but the kerb lines simply run on until they meet, which joins them exactly at any angle without a return to fit. No yellow box, no stop lines.

Nothing is paved between the roads and neither is trimmed: a structure is built carrying whichever road is higher at the crossing. The plugin does not decide the levels — raise the road that is to go over by selecting it, setting its height offset above, and applying that to the road on its own. The type and sizes come from the bridge settings further down.

A branching selection builds as one leg per run between junctions. Mitred runs each kerb line on until it crosses its neighbour and makes that crossing the corner — nothing is rounded, so a band arriving on one leg meets the same band on the next exactly, at any angle. Rounded fits a tangent arc of the return radius instead. The lines must actually meet at a shared point.

sections.name: Site & map

fields.label: Map comes from
options: OpenStreetMap — a drawing of the roads, free, no account
Satellite — aerial photography, free, no account
Cesium ion — photography, needs your own token

fields.label: Map covers this much ground
fields.placeholder: left blank: enough to cover the design

buttons.label: Put the design on the map
Trace the map’s roads into lines
Crop the map to a window

help: What this is. OpenStreetMap gives you a drawing of the roads. Cesium ion gives you aerial photographs — the real ground, which is what you want to trace a site over. It needs a free Cesium account.

What to paste. Two things, both from that account: your access token in the first box, and an asset number in the second. Leave the asset at 3954 unless you know you want another one — that is satellite imagery every account can see.

About the token. It is saved in this SketchUp file, not in the plugin. Anyone you send the file to can read it, so treat it like a password. If it goes somewhere it should not, make a new one on your Cesium account and paste that in instead.

Trace the map’s roads gives you the line down the middle of each mapped road, which is what Create builds along. Trace the road edges instead gives you both sides of each one, which is what Convert face into road wants: tidy the junctions, close each road into a face and convert it. The width of each comes from the map — what it was measured at, or its lane count, or failing both what kind of road it is called — so treat it as a starting point and drag it about.

Trace the map’s roads into lines brings the mapped roads round the site in as real SketchUp edges — centrelines already in the right place at the right size, in a group called Map Roads. Rub out what you do not want, move what you do, then select some and press Create to build roads along them. They come in as their own group rather than into the design, because a map carries footpaths, driveways and things that were never built, and what is worth keeping is your judgement to make.

Paste a link straight from Google Maps — the coordinates are read out of it — and Put the design on the map places the design there and brings the map down under it in one go. The sun and the shadows then fall as they do on site, and Street view where I click finds any point you click.

Put the map underneath is for replacing the picture on its own. It downloads the map for that spot and lays it flat under the design at its true size, on its own TerraRoad Map tag — draw the roads straight over it. By default it brings down a screenful at the zoom your link was at — six tiles across, the same sort of view you were looking at. Put a width in the box to cover a set amount of ground instead, and it zooms out as far as it must to cover it. The pasted point is taken as the middle of your design, so a plan drawn miles from the model origin still gets its own ground and not open country miles away. The map is OpenStreetMap, © OpenStreetMap contributors: Google's own tiles need a paid key and may not be fetched this way. If the network here blocks it, you are asked for a picture instead — a screenshot of the map will do, and it is sized from the zoom just the same.

If something comes out wrong, press Save a problem report straight afterwards and send me the file. It has every road and how its lines are joined, every setting, and what the plugin was asked to do in order — including anything that failed, with where it failed. A screenshot shows the wreckage; this shows what it was given.
For live aerial imagery use SketchUp's own File > Geo-location > Add Location. It cannot be opened from here, so use the menu for it.

Street view where I click opens Google Street View in your browser at that point on the design, looking the way you are looking in SketchUp — so a junction you have drawn can be held against what is actually on the ground.

fields.label: A face I draw is
options: The whole road - curb and walkway inside the line
Just the asphalt - curb and walkway outside it

rows.label: The line you drew is the road's

fields.label: Line side
options: Plot limit - keep inside the loop

rows.label: Mirror the section — turn the road round on its own line

fields.label: Mirror the section — turn the road round on its own line

help: Draw down the middle, or along either side. Choosing a side works the offset out from the section itself, so it stays right when you change the width, the footway or the verge — and any offset you type is applied on top of it. Mirroring swaps everything left for right: a footway, service road, parking bay or storm channel on one side ends up on the other, which is how you get two roads facing each other.

Loose surfaces — earthen, gravel, macadam — carry no markings, because you cannot paint a line on loose stone; they also want a steeper camber, since they shed water by shape rather than by seal. Levelling zeroes every crossfall — carriageway, shoulder, parking, verge and footway all finish at one height, so every joint closes exactly whatever the angle, at the cost of the drainage those falls were for. A negative crown gives a swale — the road drains to the middle instead of the edges. The gutter band is peeled off the road surface as its own solid so it can take a different material.

sections.name: Junctions

fields.label: Lay the shoulder round junctions
fields.title: Struck a fixed distance in from the boundary, all the way round, so it can be laid on a junction just as well as on a road. It uses the shoulder width in the Shoulder section - with the shoulder set to None there is nothing to lay, and nothing appears.

rows.label: Paint the edge line round junctions

fields.label: Paint the edge line round junctions
fields.title: Painted a fixed distance in from the boundary, not along a middle line, so a junction can carry one. A large junction usually does, marking where its running surface begins.

fields.label: Stand lamp posts round junctions
fields.title: Spaced along the curb at the same spacing the road uses, set back onto the footway, and turned to face into the junction. Never across a mouth, where a road runs in and there is no footway to stand on.

help: What a face converted as a JUNCTION carries. A junction has no line down the middle — which way the middle runs depends on which way you are going through it — so it gets none of the things laid along one: no lane markings, no parking, no median. These three need no middle line. The shoulder and the edge line are struck a fixed distance in from the boundary, and a lamp post needs a curb to stand behind, which a junction has all round its corners.

All three are off to begin with, so junctions already in your model stay exactly as they are. They are read every time a junction is built, so to put them on a junction that is already there: tick the boxes, select it, and press Repair the selected road or junction. Unlike a road, a junction takes these from this panel rather than from a style — a junction has no style of its own, it follows the roads that run into it.

Each carriageway drains away from the median. Lane count applies per direction.

help: A service road is its own road, and on the ground it stops before a junction or roundabout — its traffic joins the main carriageway first. Carried round instead, its kerbs, its planted divider and its carriageway all curve into the circle alongside the main ones, which is what reads as a doubled kerb and footway at a roundabout. Turn this off if your design really does run the service road round it.
Runs outboard of the main carriageway, separated by the divider strip. Divider curbs are taken out of the strip width, so a 2'-0" divider stays 2'-0".

Stall line height above the bay

fields.label: Stall line height above the bay

help: Bays are left off any bend curving tighter than this. A bay is a rectangle and a rectangle only fits against a straight kerb — swept round a bend it comes out wedge-shaped, the stall lines splay apart, and there is nowhere along it a car would actually sit. The bays stop before the bend and pick up again after it. Set it to 0 to lay them the whole way round regardless.

A car parked parallel needs the length of the whole kerbside space — room to get into the bay as well as sit in it — so it gets its own figure, normally 20'. The stall length above is what a bay driven into nose first needs, and is used at every other angle.

Stall lines sit a sixteenth of an inch above the bay — enough to keep the paint and the paving apart, too little to see. Road markings stand half an inch proud, which is right on a carriageway but reads as floating on a parking bay. The bay falls at its cross fall so it drains, and the stall lines painted on it fall with it — paint and ground agreeing. Tick lay the bays flat for a bay that is meant to be level instead.

Sits at road level between the carriageway and the curb. Angled bays need more depth and more kerb per car: at 45° an 8'×16' stall wants about 17'-0" of depth and 11'-4" of kerb, against 8'-0" and 16'-0" parallel.

Add a U-turn where I click

help: Edge lines are painted yellow and lane markings white, each with its own material in the list below. The studs are one component repeated, so a mile of them costs about what one costs.

Leave the deck width blank and the bridge takes the width of the road it carries, kerb to kerb, so it stays right when the road changes. Height above the ground is the clear space under the deck — how high the bridge stands.

To put a bridge in: 1. Set the type and sizes above — the span is how long the bridge will be. 2. Press Click a point on the road to add a bridge. This panel closes and SketchUp comes to the front, ready. 3. Move the mouse near the road. A red upright follows the centreline, showing exactly where the bridge will stand and which way it will face. 4. Click. The bridge is built there, centred on that point, and this panel comes back with your settings as you left them. The cursor snaps to the road, so you cannot miss it, and the road is carried over the structure. A short upright is left at the point inside the design's Bridge Markers group: drag it along the road to move the bridge, erase it and the bridge goes. Esc cancels.

The road is carried on arches, with a pier between each pair and one at each end — set how many in Arches side by side above. Where there is not the height or the length for an arch worth building, it stands on plain piers instead.

This is the other way to bridge: instead of standing a structure beside the road, it lifts the road itself. Click a point and the road climbs to the rise above, runs level across the span set above, and eases back down to the ground over the approach length at each end — so it passes over whatever is below. Put a minus in front of the rise (-16') and it goes the other way instead, dropping into an underpass. Everything the road carries — kerb, footway, markings, drainage — goes up or down with it, and the deck is built at the top. Works the same as the U-turn button: one click, and an upright is left in Level Change Markers to drag along the road or erase.

The channel is let into the edge of the carriageway against the kerb, not laid on top of it, so the paving is shortened to suit and nothing is counted twice. It is a hollow box — floor, two walls, an open void — with the GRC grating as its own part, bedded on the walls and finishing flush with the road.

Change the width where I click makes the road wider or narrower at that point — a lay-by, a bus bay, a turning head, a throat at a junction. The carriageway takes the first figure and the median the second; a minus figure narrows instead. On one side only the far kerb does not move at all — which is what a lay-by or a bus bay actually is — and two widenings on opposite sides can overlap without either taking the other's width. Everything beyond them — kerb, verge, footway, parking — moves out by what the two gained and keeps its own width. It eases in and out on a curve, so the kerb line has no step in it. The upright in Widening Markers drags along the road to move it, or rubs out to take it away.

The boxes above are only the starting point. Click the place and SketchUp's own input box opens with all four figures in it, so you can set them — or change your mind and narrow instead — before anything is built. Cancel there and nothing changes. The figures can also be typed while you are pointing, the way SketchUp's own tools take a measurement: one number for the road, or two separated by a comma for the road and the median. A bar across the road shows the width before you click — blue where it narrows, red where it widens.

The change eases in and out on a curve, and the line is resampled close enough through the taper for that curve to be built as one — a dozen or so stations across it rather than the two a long station interval would give, which is what would otherwise leave a kink in the kerb at each end.

A median cannot run into a junction — the traffic turning across it has to go somewhere — so it stops short and is capped with the same rounded end a U-turn opening gets, rather than being cut off square in mid air. Leave this at 0 for twice the median's own half width, which suits most layouts.

Click a point on a divided road and the median is opened there: its kerbs and planting stop short each side, the gap between the carriageways is paved so a vehicle can turn across, and a line is painted at each end of the opening so it reads as a turn rather than a piece of missing median. The upright left behind can be dragged along the road to move the turn, or erased to take it away. Needs a road with a median.

A rounded hump swept across the carriageway as a real solid, flat where it meets the road so there is no step at either foot. The markings are the same shape laid a hair proud, so they follow the hump rather than cutting through it.

Markings are laid on the surface like tape at the height above road. Centre lines, dividers and edge lines each keep their own width and pattern. The stop line crosses the approaching half of the carriageway only, so which side traffic keeps to decides which half it covers.

help: A transmission line is not street lighting and does not share its settings. It can run along a road — down the median, or outside the kerb on either side — or pass through the site on its own, off the road altogether.

Leave the offset at 0 and the supports stand just outside the kerb on the side chosen. Three conductors on each arm puts one over the pole, which is what a three-phase arm looks like; two puts one at each end.

Line from lines I have drawn puts a transmission line along something you have drawn anywhere — with any SketchUp tool — whether or not there is a road under it. Select what you drew and press the button.

fields.label: Stands on
options: A set distance behind the curb

help: The transmission tower is a lattice pylon: four splayed legs cross-braced the whole way up, three levels of crossarm with an insulator string under each tip, and an earth peak above. Conductors are slung between consecutive towers and sag into the span as real ones do — the arm length sets how far the crossarms reach, and the pole height the whole tower. Set the spacing wide: towers stand hundreds of feet apart, not tens.

The butterfly type is always twin-armed — a single arm would leave its brace holding nothing. A double arm carries a head each way — what a pole standing in a median needs, and how one line of poles lights a road from the middle.

sections.name: Zebra crossings
help: Bars run parallel to the traffic and are centred across each carriageway, so a crossing never ends on a sliver against the kerb.
